items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The mention of Maynard Ferguson occurs entirely within the [INTERVIEWER]'s turn, where the interviewer lists Wayne Shorter's past bands. The interviewee does not mention Maynard Ferguson, nor does she respond to the specific mention of him with any personal anecdote or relationship description.

ctx.x: Now I understand a little more. There’s something that really does bother me a lot. That is that somebody you don’t know will put out a CD with all their original tunes. I see this all the time. I’ve got three or four CDs. One guy wrote to me. He’s a very good piano player. He’s just finished college. He’s going out. He says in his letter that he wants to start performing. He sent me a CD, and they’re all his own tunes except one, and I don’t know why he picked it. “It Might As Well Be Spring.” I hear so many…

It’s so important. I agree. And I think that a lot of that might be that it’s been encouraged that they don’t know the history of Wayne Shorter, that he spent many years playing standards, doing this, and playing with, played with Art Blakey for six years, played with Miles for four years, and played with Maynard Ferguson, and did all kind . . . Horace Silver . . . did a whole range of things before he was able to evolve to even do his first recording. And even his first recordings wasn’t just original…

I feel that these guys, that they’re not thinking it through and nobody has told them. Or I’m thinking, do they think their tunes are so good? Or do they want the money from the royalties? How many records is a guy going to sell that nobody ever heard of? How’s he going to get going?
